title: Emotions and the brain
examples: How does my brain know when I am scared?
Can I teach myself to feel less angry?
What part of the brain controls my emotions?

explain.say: Emotions are natural reactions to things happening around you.
They help us survive and connect with other people safely.

draw.text: Emotions help us survive and connect.

explain.say: Learning to name your feelings helps you understand them better.

items: Understand it (e.g., I need a break)

explain.say: When you feel overwhelmed, taking deep breaths can calm your body.
If you feel angry, instead of shouting, try walking away for a moment.
A common mistake is thinking that all big feelings are bad feelings.

faq.a: We have emotions because they are signals from our brain. They tell us what we need to pay attention to.
asks: What is the purpose of feelings?

faq.q: How do I know what I am feeling?
faq.a: Try pausing and asking yourself what physical sensations you notice. Naming the feeling helps you understand it.
asks: What helps me name my feelings?

faq.q: What is the best way to calm down?
faq.a: Deep, slow breathing is a very effective way to calm your nervous system. It tells your body that you are safe.
asks: How do I calm down quickly?

faq.q: Do I have to feel happy all the time?
faq.a: No, it is normal to feel a wide range of emotions. Every feeling has a purpose.
asks: Is it okay to feel sad?

faq.q: Does my brain change how I react to emotions?
faq.a: Yes, practicing calming techniques helps train your brain over time. It builds new, healthier responses.
asks: How does practice help my emotions?

facts: Emotions are complex reactions involving thoughts and body signals.
The amygdala is a part of the brain involved in processing emotions.
Deep breathing can activate the body's relaxation response.
Understanding emotions is key to emotional intelligence.

quiz.say: When you feel worried about a test, what is the best first step?
quiz.show: Deep breathing is the first step.

options.show: Deep breathing is the first step.
options.say: Deep breathing is the first step.

quiz.why: Deep breathing helps calm your body's immediate stress response.

wrong.0: This makes the feeling stronger because you do not process it.
wrong.1: Talking is good, but you need to calm your body first to talk clearly.
wrong.2: Running away avoids the feeling but does not solve the underlying issue.

quiz.say: If you feel frustrated because a puzzle is hard, what should you try?
quiz.show: Name the feeling, then take a break.

options.show: Getting angry at the puzzle pieces.
options.say: Getting angry at the puzzle pieces.

options.show: Asking a friend to solve it for you.
options.say: Asking a friend to solve it for you.

options.show: Name the feeling, then take a break.
options.say: Name the feeling, then take a break.

options.show: Forcing yourself to finish it right away.
options.say: Forcing yourself to finish it right away.

quiz.why: Naming the feeling gives it a label, and taking a break allows your brain to reset.

wrong.0: Anger at objects does not help you solve the puzzle.
wrong.1: While help is good, you miss the chance to practice your own problem-solving.
wrong.3: Forcing it when frustrated often leads to more mistakes.

quiz.say: What is the main purpose of having emotions?

options.show: To make us feel good all the time.
options.say: To make us feel good all the time.

options.show: To show other people how we think.
options.say: To show other people how we think.

quiz.why: They are signals that help us react appropriately to our environment.

wrong.0: If they only made us feel good, we would not know when danger is near.
wrong.1: While they communicate, their primary role is internal survival and guidance.
wrong.2: This is too simple; they are complex tools for interaction and survival.
